status_summary: On 2025-03-31 the Eastern District of Texas, in consolidated suits by laboratory groups (American Clinical Laboratory Association v. FDA, No. 4:24-cv-00479), vacated FDA's May 2024 laboratory-developed test rule in full, holding that FDA lacks authority to regulate laboratory-developed test services, and remanded to HHS. Trade and legal sources report that FDA did not appeal. On 2025-09-19 FDA published a final rule, effective that day, that removes the 2024 wording on laboratory manufacturers from 21 CFR 809.3(a), restoring the earlier text. Later, H.R. 8890 (Enhancing CLIA Act of 2026) was introduced on 2026-05-19 and referred to two House committees; its introduced text would regulate laboratory-developed tests under CLIA rather than as devices under the FDCA, with provisions on performing a test in commonly owned laboratories and on tests that modify FDA-regulated products, and no action beyond referral is listed. On 2026-07-16 CMS published a request for information on CLIA regulations (comments due 2026-09-14) that asks about performance specifications for non-cleared and modified tests. The test-sharing mechanism and revised rules for modified tests that the document recommends are not yet enacted or adopted.

timeline.event: The Eastern District of Texas, in American Clinical Laboratory Association v. FDA (No. 4:24-cv-00479) consolidated with Association for Molecular Pathology v. FDA (No. 4:24-cv-00824), entered final judgment vacating and setting aside FDA's laboratory-developed test final rule in its entirety, after holding in its memorandum opinion that the rule exceeds FDA's authority under the FDCA, and remanded to HHS.
timeline.source: U.S. District Court, E.D. Tex. (judgment copy hosted by ARUP Laboratories)

timeline.event: FDA publishes a final rule implementing the vacatur by removing the 2024 phrase on laboratory manufacturers from 21 CFR 809.3(a), effective on publication.

H.R. 8890, the Enhancing CLIA Act of 2026 (Enhancing Clinical Laboratory Innovation and Access Act of 2026), was introduced by Rep. Neal Dunn and referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees; no cosponsors or later action are listed. The introduced text would regulate laboratory-developed tests under CLIA rather than as devices under the FDCA.

CMS, with CDC, publishes a request for information on CLIA regulations (91 FR 43586, docket CMS-3485-NC), with comments due 2026-09-14; it asks about establishing performance specifications for tests that are not FDA-cleared and about modifications to FDA-cleared systems, and does not itself resolve the FDA and CLIA split.

title: Reform FDA oversight of laboratory-developed tests
uncertainties: The outcome follows a court ruling that FDA implemented rather than an agency reform designed to the document's terms, so alignment is partial. The absence of an FDA appeal rests on two trade and legal reports (Becker's, Manatt); no court docket or FDA statement was opened, and the appeal date cited by Manatt is its own calculation. Bill content is taken from the introduced text on govinfo, read through a summarizing fetch; the BILLSTATUS record lists only introduction and referral, no CRS summary and no cosponsors, and no Senate companion was confirmed. The court judgment and opinion were read through copies hosted by a laboratory company and by a plaintiff association that carry the court's filing headers (Documents 94 and 93, filed 2025-03-31); the court docket itself could not be opened. The CMS request for information was read on the Federal Register page: it touches performance specifications for non-cleared and modified tests but does not use the term laboratory-developed test and is not treated as a reform of the FDA and CLIA split. A CMS proposed rule on CLIA published 2026-10-08 was only partly read and was not found to address laboratory-developed tests. A Federal Register search for FDA documents on laboratory-developed tests after 2025-09-19 returned none. Searches were limited in number and absence of other guidance is not proven.
